extracted.intended_audience: researchers, funders, research institutions, and others interested in preprints and open/post-publication peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Operating a publishing platform that posts preprints immediately and then conducts formal, invited post-publication peer review; includes pre-publication checks, referee selection, structured review reports, versioning, indexing thresholds, and reviewer credit mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Following article submission, an internal team (largely postdocs) conduct a series of pre-publication checks. These are significantly more rigorous than those typically conducted on traditional preprint servers and more closely resemble those found in journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checks include whether it is scientific work from a scientist; whether it is plagiarised; whether it meets ethical requirements; whether it is readable and meets community standards; whether we have source data (which we require); and whether it adheres to FAIR principles. F1000 reports a median of 2 working days for these checks and ~75–86% acceptance rates depending on platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for source data and FAIR adherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Source data (which we require) and adherence to FAIR principles are assessed as part of the pre-publication checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must provide source data; the platform checks for FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) compliance. Lack of required documentation or data can cause rejection at this stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication as a citable, well-typed record
rubrics_metrics.description: All articles that pass the checks are published with a DOI (i.e. citable) and are typeset with NLM-compliant XML and associated with detailed metadata to maximise readability, accessibility and text mining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production (including author proofing) takes a median of 4–5 working days; overall median submission-to-publication time is 14–16 working days. Unlike many preprint servers, published items are produced to journal-like standards for indexing and discoverability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author commitment to invited post-publication peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: At the time of submission, the authors commit themselves to immediate formal, post publication, invited peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this commitment, authors cannot send the article to a journal after posting; the model is author-driven but bound to the invited peer review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee selection and vetting
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors select referees from a list provided or suggest others; the internal team checks all selected referees for relevant experience and obvious conflicts of interest, and then invite the approved referees on the authors’ behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite concerns, recruiting reviewers has not been harder; the average number of reviewers invited for articles that have 'passed' peer review is 10. The internal vetting step is explicit and required to ensure suitability and manage conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee response format: approval statuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees are asked to do two things: provide a status (approved; approved with reservations; not approved), and a supporting referee report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The explicit three-way status is used both to summarise judgement and to determine indexing thresholds. Referees are guided through structured forms to provide both the status and detailed technical commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured, technical peer review questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees are guided through structured forms to consider specific aspects of the article, depending on article type; the peer review questions are focussed on technical aspects of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific focus areas include the appropriateness of study designs and methods, and the extent of support for conclusions drawn. F1000 is also developing tools to assess perceived impact and importance of findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and transparency of referee reports
rubrics_metrics.description: The referee reports are published alongside the article and are signed with the referees’ names and affiliations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports are fully public (open peer review), which F1000 reports leads to more candid, constructive reviews. Reports receive DOIs and can be cited and added to ORCID and Publons profiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer credit and recognition mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review activity is enabled to obtain credit: DOIs on every report (making them citable), and enabling (and indeed encouraging) inclusion of these reports on ORCID profiles and in Publons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encouragement to list co-referees supports recognition of early career researchers who often contribute substantially. F1000 notes growth in co-referee listing from 4% to 12% (2013–2017) and large numbers of referee reports recorded on ORCID.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revisions, versioning, and author control
rubrics_metrics.description: With this author-driven approach, the authors decide whether, how and when they wish to respond to the referees and whether they want to revise. New versions are published and are added to the history of the article but are independently citable; referees can update their approval status with each version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article title updates dynamically with version number and referee status. Any researcher can comment throughout the process. There is no final unchangeable version of the article; authors control when to stop changing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing threshold for bibliographic databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Indexing in major bibliographic databases (e.g., PubMed, Scopus) is contingent on referee statuses: once an article achieves two 'Approved' statuses, or one 'Approved' and two 'Approved with Reservations', it is indexed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexers then index all versions, past and future. This provides a clear, stated threshold linking peer review outcomes to formal indexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hands-on editorial/logistical support to speed review
rubrics_metrics.description: F1000's internal team manages the logistical aspects of the whole process, which they believe makes peer review very fast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing administrative/editorial support, active referee finding, and enabling reviewers to receive credit are cited as reasons for faster turnaround and higher reviewer participation. Median times for checks and production are reported; the model emphasizes active management rather than passive hosting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology and infrastructure to support complex versioned publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Robust technological infrastructure is required to handle article versions and the complexity of the workflow, and to maximise links with scholarly infrastructure providers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems include referee finders, referee report authoring systems, tools for authors to respond and update articles, integration with ORCID, CrossRef, repositories, indexers, impact & analysis tools, and support for metadata and machine-readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency as a core principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency (open peer review, published signed reports, version histories) is described as a crucial part of the approach, bringing significant benefits to authors, referees and readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: F1000 reports transparency leads to reviewers taking the process more seriously and provides more constructive reviews; openness underpins credit mechanisms and encourages community engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-driven governance and researcher control
rubrics_metrics.description: F1000 positions its role as a service provider rather than controller: researchers themselves are in charge of their article and make the key decisions (no Editors making decisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The platform's processes and evolution are intended to be responsive to community needs; operational control (logistics, vetting, indexing thresholds) is provided as a service while final editorial choices remain with authors.
